data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI gap is best explained by differential longwave radiative cooling driven by emissivity and surface properties: urban materials have different emissivity and thermal admittance than natural surfaces, causing cities to cool more slowly after sunset, and the gap scales with impervious surface fraction.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If urban emissivity is not significantly lower than rural emissivity, the emissivity component fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI gap does not scale with impervious surface fraction across cities, thermal admittance alone is insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If material emissivity variations are dwarfed by sky view factor effects, this mechanism is secondary.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"After sunset, longwave radiative cooling dominates the surface energy balance. Urban impervious surfaces with high thermal admittance resist temperature change, releasing stored heat gradually. The lower emissivity of some urban materials compared to vegetation and soil can further slow radiative loss. The cross-city magnitude depends on impervious surface fraction and material emissivity: cities with more impervious, low-emissivity surfaces maintain a larger nocturnal temperature excess.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
